78: Our base is a permitted commissary, and we do not try to build a kitchen of our own. It is where the cart and the portable bar get ready for every event: we fill the fresh water tanks, empty the gray water at an approved point, keep the milk and the cold brew in refrigeration, store the dry goods and cups, and park the trailer between bookings. The example budgets {{alquiler_mes}} per month for all of it. Published rates for shared kitchens typically run from $15 to $45 an hour depending on the city and the equipment, according to The Food Corridor, so we compare at least three commissaries on price, on hours that fit an early loading time on event mornings, on cooler space and on trailer parking. Before paying a deposit we sign a written commissary agreement that spells out our hours, our shelves and refrigeration, where the gear is stored, cleaning duties, insurance requirements and notice for ending the arrangement, and where the county asks for it we keep a commissary log. The rule we follow is simple: own what travels to the event and rent what you use a few days a week.
79: The equipment list follows the order in which we buy it. First comes what the county and the venue decide: the plan review for the cart and the power. A two-group machine at 220V and 3,400 W needs a dedicated circuit (NEMA 6-20), while a standard 110V outlet only runs a compact machine, so the first move is a question to the health department and an electrician, not a purchase. Second come the two stations: the espresso cart ({{inv_carro}}), the portable espresso bar for the second station ({{inv_barra}}), the espresso machines ({{inv_espresso}}) and four grinders, a house grinder and a decaf grinder at each station ({{inv_molinos}}). Third comes what keeps them running: the inverter generator, cords and power distribution ({{inv_energia}}), plus the batch brewer, airpots and cold brew system ({{inv_brew}}). Last come the enclosed trailer ({{inv_remolque}}) with its wrap, hitch and ramps ({{inv_remolque_wrap}}). The tow vehicle is the one the owner already has, so it is not in the budget.
80: Every event follows the same script, and we write it before we sell the first date. About three weeks out we hold the final planning call with the host to confirm service hours, drinks, allergies, the outlet or the generator, and where the trailer parks; the host gives us the final guest count about ten days before the event. About two weeks out we check the room: the power, the distance to the cart, the access route and the parking. The day before, at the commissary, we make the cold brew and the syrups and chill the milk. On the day we load, drive, set up in about an hour, warm up the machines and dial in the grinders, serve for two to two and a half hours (55.3% of real bookings are two-hour events, according to Flashquotes), break down and clean. That is why a two-hour event takes 7 to 9 hours of shift, according to GrindKit, and why we budget it that way. One barista makes 50 to 65 drinks an hour at most, according to Flashquotes, so the number of baristas follows the guest count.
81: Quality and safety are two different jobs. For quality, every double uses 18 g (0.63 oz) of coffee at a 1:2 ratio, which gives about 23 net doubles from a pound after purging and dialing in (kit estimate). Plan about 1.0 drinks per guest for a service of up to two hours, 1.3 to 1.5 for two to four hours, and 20-30% more in the morning, according to GrindKit. For safety, milk is a time and temperature control food, so we hold it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit) in the cart's refrigerator and in coolers, and we check it with a thermometer. Each milk gets its own pitcher, and we purge the steam wand between milks. Handwashing comes first, and we wipe the wand after every drink and rinse the portafilters between services. Milk, soy, tree nuts and, in pastries, wheat and egg go on every quote as allergens.
82: The supply chain is short, and we keep a backup for each item. Coffee comes from a specialty roaster that sells wholesale: the example uses about $14 a pound, between the national retail average of $9.33 a pound (BLS) and about $18 a pound for wholesale specialty beans. Whole milk averages $4.11 a gallon (BLS), and oat milk comes from a restaurant distributor or a cash-and-carry. Compostable cups, lids and sleeves come from a packaging supplier, and any pastries come from a licensed bakery. A local technician services the espresso machines on a schedule, and the water filters are changed on a calendar. Keep a small box of spares, such as gaskets, a portafilter basket and a steam wand tip, because a machine that fails in the middle of a service costs more than the part.
85: The team is small, and every role has a clear job. The owner is the lead barista and the salesperson, who also books, buys and serves at the events that matter most. A lead barista, a part-time hourly W-2 employee, runs the second station and covers the big events. Event baristas are hourly W-2 employees who work event by event, and an on-call barista who doubles as the driver covers the peak months. There is no dining room, no front-of-house manager and no office, so payroll flexes with the calendar and the events pay for the structure.
86: Labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, which is {{personal_pct}} of sales. That figure includes the owner's pay and the employer payroll taxes for everyone on the payroll. It is the largest cost in the plan, and it moves with the calendar: in a March with two conferences everyone works, and in July almost nobody does. The owner's pay and the lead barista's pay are fixed, while event barista cost depends on the hours of each event. If you book fewer events than planned, you schedule fewer hours and the cost drops; if you book more, you carry them with the same people until the coverage runs out and then add someone to the payroll, never a contractor who invoices you by the event. Change the "Staffing" sheet to your own wage rates before you show this plan to a lender.
87: Every event takes hours of loading, travel, setup, service, breakdown and cleaning. The workbook assumes {{horas_evento}} hours per person and {{personas_evento}} baristas per event on average, and it compares the hours scheduled with the hours needed to give a coverage of {{cobertura_horas}}. One cart with one barista serves 50 to 65 drinks an hour, and two stations with two baristas about 100, according to Flashquotes, so weddings and large corporate events get two baristas. High coverage does not mean you have too many people. It means the roster can carry a busy week, such as two corporate events and a Saturday wedding. The workbook spreads payroll evenly over the 12 months, which is conservative given the summer dip.
88: Everyone but the owner is a W-2 employee. Event baristas work under our direction, on our schedule and with our equipment, which is the profile the Fair Labor Standards Act treats as employment, and California's AB5 presumes it. Calling them contractors may look cheaper, but misclassification can bring back taxes, penalties and claims, and it can sink a loan application. Payroll taxes add {{cargas_pct}} to wages in the model, workers' compensation is required in nearly every state, and you pay at least the highest of the federal, state and local minimum wage; the workbook uses the federal floor of {{salario_minimo_federal}} for full-time work as its reference, and many states are higher. For wages, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (OEWS, May 2025) has no occupation of its own for baristas, who sit inside Fast Food and Counter Workers (35-3023), with a median of $15.00 an hour, a 75th percentile of $17.34 and a 90th percentile of $20.51. Event baristas earn more: $20 to $35 an hour according to GrindKit, and $25 in the Flashquotes model, plus voluntary tips. Check your city before you set rates.
89: Training is part of the plan, not an extra. The owner or the lead barista holds a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe Manager where the county asks for one, and every barista gets the food handler card that your state or county requires. Beyond the paperwork we train three things. The first is drink standards: dose, ratio, milk texture, latte art and the house recipes, so the last cup of a service tastes like the first. The second is speed on the line, so the queue never stalls. The third is safety: milk temperature, allergens such as milk, soy and tree nuts, steam burns, and handling the generator and the cords. Before the first event of the season, the crew runs a full rehearsal at the commissary with both stations set up and a timer running. The rehearsal costs a morning and shows you what is missing from the load list before a host does.
90: Handle the service charge and the gratuity differently, because the IRS does. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge that the host must pay is treated as wages to the staff who receive it, so payroll taxes apply. A gratuity is voluntary, the amount is the guest's choice and it belongs to the baristas. A tip jar at the cart works only if the host accepts it, and it belongs to the team too. We list the service charge and any gratuity on separate lines of the quote, say plainly what each one pays for and distribute gratuities under a written policy. Check your state's overtime rules as well, because a wedding that ends late after an early setup is a long shift. Whether the service charge is subject to sales tax depends on your state, which the legal section covers.
93: Taken together, the case describes a small business that is viable on paper. Year-1 sales are {{ventas_a1}}, the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}} and EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. The average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}, which sits inside the range Flashquotes reports for real bookings, with a median of $1,040. These are planning figures from the workbook, not a forecast: they hold as long as you book the events in the plan at the average price of the mix. That average includes the corporate drop-offs and small office breaks, which sell for less, so it is not the price of a wedding. The next sections show where each number comes from.
94: The investment is built from lines you can price today. The two stations come first: the espresso cart ({{inv_carro}}), the portable espresso bar ({{inv_barra}}), the espresso machines ({{inv_espresso}}) and the grinders ({{inv_molinos}}). Then come the enclosed trailer ({{inv_remolque}}), the power setup ({{inv_energia}}), the website, photos, tastings and launch ({{inv_lanzamiento}}), the opening inventory ({{inv_stock}}), the first-year permits and certifications ({{inv_permisos}}) and the county plan review ({{inv_plan_review}}). Startup costs also include a 10% contingency on the cart, the portable bar, the trailer, its fit-out and the plan review, and they add up to {{capex}}. On top we set aside working capital of {{fondo_maniobra}}, which covers the first months while payments come in, for a total investment of {{inversion_total}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. A loan of that size means a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, not a Microloan, which tops out at $50,000. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is not guaranteed: the terms are an illustration, not an offer, so get quotes for the cart, the machines and the trailer before you treat any figure as closed.
95: Revenue grows with the number of events, not with the price. The workbook raises events by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{eventos_a1}} to about {{eventos_a2}} and then {{eventos_a3}} (the workbook keeps the annual averages with decimals), at the same price per guest and the same guests per event. That takes sales from {{ventas_a1}} in year 1 to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3, and net profit from {{resultado_neto_a1}} to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. Growth in events is realistic only if repeat business builds: companies that reorder, venues and planners that send you bookings and couples who recommend you. The model applies an income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}} as a reserve; with a pass-through LLC the owner pays that tax on a personal return, so keeping the reserve is the prudent choice. Capacity matters too, because two stations and a handful of baristas can only cover so many events.
96: The cost structure can be checked against reference ranges. The cost of goods on coffee bar package sales is {{coste_paquetes_pct}}, and all goods together are {{cogs_pct}} of sales. Compostable cups, lids, sleeves and napkins add {{consumibles_pct}}. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales, and the commissary, cart storage and trailer parking are {{ocupacion_pct}}, or {{ocupacion_anual}} a year. Marketing is {{marketing_anual}} a year, insurance is {{seguros_anual}} and year-1 interest is {{intereses_a1}}. For reference, GrindKit puts the all-in cost per drink at $0.75 to $1.50, with a cost of goods of 20-30% of drink revenue; package revenue also pays for the baristas, so goods are a smaller share here. Flashquotes describes operator gross margins of 50-70% after the event staff; this plan's {{margen_bruto_pct}} is before labor, and once the event baristas are paid it falls back into that range. If your cost per drink sits above that range, check your dose, your milk waste and your cup prices first.
97: Break-even is measured in events per year. On an accounting basis the business covers its costs with {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. On a cash basis, with loan payments in and depreciation out, it needs {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}}, against {{eventos_a1}} in the plan. That leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even: events can fall {{caida_absorbible_pct}} before cash stops covering costs. It is a real cushion, but not a wide one, and a slow summer can eat it. The workbook shows the exact figure and the plan rounds up to whole events. Track it every month.
98: You can fail on cash even when the profit looks good. The workbook assumes you collect from clients in {{cobro_dias}} days on average and pay suppliers in {{pago_dias}} days, with payroll going out every month. The lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} (September in the example, which opens in March), after the summer dip and the sales tax payment due that month (the model settles in June, September and December). The lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}} and the payback before debt is {{payback}}. Retainers are not modeled, so real cash should be a little better.
99: Two scenarios show how fast the numbers move. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_eventos}} events at {{pesimista_invitados}} guests and {{pesimista_precio}} per guest, which gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. Year-1 closing cash comes out at {{pesimista_caja}}: the cash runs out, narrowly, and you would need more equity, a credit line or lower spending before you get there. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_ventas}} with {{optimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. Remember that {{eventos_a1}} events is the pace of a full-time operator with an active corporate sales effort, not the average first year. With a thin cushion you have four levers: book more corporate events, adjust the price, add guests per event and negotiate more time with your lender. The workbook rules: if you change a green cell, this document falls behind.
102: You cannot run a coffee catering business from your home kitchen, and the commissary is the legal anchor of this plan. A cart is a mobile food unit in states such as Washington and Indiana and a mobile food facility in California, and the process is the same as for a food truck. The FDA Food Code leaves the commissary decision to the local authority. California's Health and Safety Code (section 114295) generally requires a mobile food facility to operate in conjunction with an approved commissary or other approved facility, and Snohomish County, Washington, requires one, with an annual agreement and a commissary log on board, unless a state exemption applies. So the answer is usually yes, and some counties exempt self-contained units: ask yours in writing before you buy the cart. This section is general information, not legal advice.
103: With the commissary secured, the next layer is the health permit. Expect a mobile food unit permit and a plan review from your county, and ask for the plan review before you buy the cart. As one example we read, Snohomish County charges $1,100 for the plan review and $500, $745 or $1,025 a year for the permit depending on risk, and it wants the electrical approval first. Beyond that you need a business license, a sales tax permit, food handler cards for the whole team and, in some counties, a Certified Food Protection Manager; each festival or market may also ask for a temporary event permit. Milk is a time and temperature control food, so the cart needs an approved refrigerator that holds it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit), plus a handwashing sink with hot water and water tanks sized to your county's rule: check your county.
104: Power is the question to ask first and the one most owners check last. A two-group machine at 220V and 3,400 W needs a dedicated circuit (NEMA 6-20, 15 to 17 A), so our checklist asks every room the same thing: 110V or 220V, how many amps and how far from the cart. If the room cannot deliver, the answer is an inverter generator of about 5,500 W. A coffee cart makes no grease-laden vapors, so it does not usually need a Type I hood, but the generator has its own rules. As one example, a city fire department checklist (Lenexa, Kansas, based on NFPA 96) asks for a free-standing generator at least 12 ft (3.7 m) from the unit and 10 ft (3 m) from buildings, with an extinguisher on hand, and some states, such as New Jersey, may require a fire safety permit where a generator is used. Ask your fire marshal before you buy, and never assume that no permit is needed.
105: What we serve has its own rules. Pastries come only from a licensed bakery: cottage food laws let a home baker sell directly to the consumer, and reselling through a business is usually outside them, so check your state and never assume that cottage food pastries are fine. Cups are a local rule: the kit budgets compostable cups, and Seattle, as an example, requires single-use compostable items on site and has banned foam since 2009, while your city may say something different. There is no alcohol in this plan: an espresso martini needs a liquor license, so we partner with a licensed mobile bar. Declare the allergens on every quote: milk, soy and tree nuts such as almond and, in pastries, wheat and egg are among the nine major U.S. allergens, which also include sesame. Oat milk counts as gluten-free only if it is labeled gluten-free.
106: Sales tax depends on who pays. A hosted event is catering, and in many states, such as California and New York, the whole invoice is taxed, including staff and extras, and in some states travel. At festivals and farmers markets, where each guest pays for a drink, tax is charged drink by drink and may need a registration where you sell. Rate and taxability depend on your state and on who pays. Register for a sales tax permit; the workbook applies {{sales_tax}} to the whole invoice, which is the conservative choice. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge is wages, not a tip, while a gratuity and a tip jar the host accepts are voluntary and belong to the team.
107: Hiring and insurance come next. Event baristas belong on W-2 payroll with workers' compensation (optional only in Texas, where venues and lenders still ask for it), Form I-9, Form W-4 and your state's new-hire reporting. The FLSA treats them as employees in almost every case, and California's AB5 presumes it, so a 1099 is a risk. The example budgets a lean {{seguros_anual}} a year (get quotes) for general liability of $1M/$2M with unlimited additional insureds, commercial auto that covers the trailer, workers' compensation and equipment in transit. Venues will ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as an additional insured. There is no alcohol in the plan, so there is no liquor liability.
108: The last link is the road. The trailer is titled and registered with your state DMV in the business name, and the tow vehicle needs the towing capacity and the hitch for a loaded 6 by 12 ft enclosed trailer, so check the ratings before you buy and make sure your commercial auto policy covers the trailer. If you have no suitable tow vehicle, a used van costs about $18,000 and is not in the budget. If you operate in the UK, the rules differ: register your food business with the local council at least 28 days before you start trading, get a street trading licence or consent to sell on the street, expect a Food Hygiene Rating from 0 to 5 (the FHIS in Scotland), declare the 14 listed allergens, charge VAT on event catering once you are VAT-registered, and read the NCASS guidance for mobile coffee.
111: The plan holds up because of how it is built. There is no storefront to lease or fit out: the cart and the portable bar travel in one trailer, the commissary handles water, cold storage and parking, and a short drink list with a low cost per drink leaves a high gross margin. Two stations let us serve a conference floor or a wedding cocktail hour without a line, and weekday companies fill the calendar that weddings leave open. The case is viable: sales of {{ventas_a1}}, net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a lowest DSCR of {{dscr_min}} and a payback of {{payback}}. But be honest about the limits. The cushion over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}, July is the slowest month for coffee carts, according to Flashquotes, corporate clients concentrate the risk, {{eventos_a1}} events is a full-time operator's pace and in the pessimistic case the cash runs out. If volume stalls, you have the levers: more corporate events, price, guests per event and more time with your lender.
112: Know the risks before you sign anything. A late cancellation is handled with the retainer and the cancellation tiers in the contract. A room with no 220V outlet is handled by asking in writing, by running a compact machine on 110V or by bringing the generator. Rain at an outdoor event is handled with a canopy or by moving inside, and the contract says rain is not force majeure. Milk out of temperature is the risk that can hurt a guest: it is prevented with a refrigerator and coolers that hold 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit), a thermometer and a rule that warm milk goes in the trash. A machine that fails mid-service is handled by the second station and a service contract with a technician. A slow July is handled with farmers markets, festivals and a cash reserve of about three months. A shortage of baristas in peak months is handled with a bench of trained part-time W-2 employees. Inspections hold no surprises if your permits, logs and commissary agreement are in order.
113: Our strengths come from the service itself. We sell a short, well-tested list and make every drink fresh in front of the guests. Two stations and about 100 drinks an hour let us serve a large reception without a line, and oat milk is included in the price. Branded cups and latte printing give companies something to photograph. A permitted commissary, written allergen handling, a contract with clear tiers and a certificate of insurance ready to send give planners, venues and office managers the reassurance they look for. Fixed costs stay low because we share the commissary and run one trailer, so a slow month hurts less. And our best sales argument is not price. It is the first good latte at eight in the morning in a conference room that never had one.
114: The roadmap follows the six phases of the startup checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" covers the LLC, the tax registrations, the bank account, the loan application and your contract. "Phase 2 - Permits & Commissary" covers the commissary agreement, the county plan review and health permit, the fire marshal and generator questions, the cart order and the insurance, in that order. "Phase 3 - Equipment" covers the machines, the grinders, the trailer, the brewing gear and a full test run with both stations. "Phase 4 - Staff" covers W-2 hiring, payroll and barista training. "Phase 5 - Marketing" builds the website, the Google Business Profile, the listings on The Knot, Zola and GigSalad, the outreach to planners, venues and office managers and the first tastings. "Phase 6 - First 90 Days" runs the first events and reviews each one against the plan. The phases overlap week by week, but do not book a paid event while any permit is still open.
115: Measure a few things every week and do not wait for your accountant. Track events booked per month and the share of quotes that become signed bookings: 20-30% is normal, according to Flashquotes, and much more than that suggests your price is too low. Compare your average price per guest, excluding sales tax, with the {{precio_invitado}} in the plan, remembering that it is an average of the mix. Track drinks per guest and drinks per barista hour, your cost per drink and your cost of goods against the {{cogs_pct}} in the plan, and the labor hours per event against the workbook. Log cancellations, events where rain or a power problem changed the plan, and the reviews you collect. Each month, compare your cash balance with the lowest balance in the workbook, {{saldo_minimo}}. If three weeks go by without a signed event, do not wait for the end of the quarter: review your price, your outreach and your calendar.
116: Over three years, the plan is to build a base of clients who come back: companies that reorder, planners and venues that recommend us and couples who refer their friends. That smooths the calendar and lowers the sales cost of every event, while events grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3. Sales reach {{ventas_a3}} and net profit {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3. A third station or a second trailer makes sense only when the peak-season calendar is full and you are turning down dates, not before. A coffee shop of your own is a different business with different numbers, and it makes sense only if your results ask for it; the Coffee Shop Business Plan Kit is the next step if they do. Meanwhile, growth comes from filling the events you already have more profitably: more guests per event, better add-ons such as branded cups and more repeat bookings.
117: The next steps are simple, and they go in order. Open the Excel workbook and replace the example figures with yours in the green cells: events per year, price per guest and guests per event. If you change one of them, this document falls behind, so the workbook rules. Use the pricing calculator, with its "Cost per Drink" and "Pricing Calculator" sheets, to turn your costs into quotes you can send, use the contract template for your bookings and use the checklist so no permit gets skipped. This plan is a planning tool, not legal or tax advice: confirm what applies to you with your accountant, your county health department and your fire marshal. And keep an eye on year 1, when the loan payment is already running and the cushion over cash break-even is thinnest ({{holgura_caja_pct}}, rising in years 2 and 3).
